en: The Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai, while expounding the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, said:
"As for the Single Ultimate Truth (*eka-paramārtha-satya*), there is no duality;
because there is no duality, it is called the Single Ultimate Truth. Furthermore, the Single Ultimate Truth is named 'free from falsehood'; furthermore, the Single Ultimate Truth..."
It is free from inversion;
furthermore, this single ultimate truth is not that which was spoken by Māra;
moreover, this single ultimate truth is termed permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
The [truths of] permanence, bliss, self, and purity do not differ from emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.
To differ would be duality; because of duality, they would not be the one true reality.
The one true reality is precisely emptiness, precisely the provisional, and precisely the middle—without difference and without duality; therefore, it is called the one true reality.
If there were three distinctions, it would be deceptive; that which is deceptive is not called the One True Reality.
Because there are no three distinctions, it is the One True Reality.
If they were different, then inversion would not have been eliminated and there would be no single ultimate truth;
because there are no three differences, there is no inversion, and because there is no inversion, it is called the single ultimate truth.
If these were different, they would not be called the One Vehicle;
because these three dharmas are non-different, complete, and perfect, they are named the One Vehicle.
This vehicle is lofty and vast, adorned with all manner of jewels; therefore, it is called the Single Truth of Reality.
Although Māra does not personally realize the distinctness of emptiness and the provisional, he is nonetheless able to speak of the distinctness of emptiness and the provisional;
yet if emptiness, the provisional, and the Middle Way were not distinct, Māra would be unable to speak of them. That which Māra cannot speak of is called the one true reality (*ekābhūtārtha*).

If emptiness, the provisional, and the middle were different, they would be called inverted; if they are not different, they are called non-inverted. Because they are non-inverted, there are no afflictions;
because there are no afflictions, it is called purity. Because there are no afflictions, there is no karma;
because there is no karma, it is called self. Because there is no karma, there is no retribution; because there is no retribution, it is called bliss.
Without retribution, there is no birth and death; without birth and death, it is called "constant.
This permanence, bliss, self, and purity is termed the One True Reality.
The One True Reality is precisely the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
The true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the very essence of the sūtra.
This true reality consists of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle:
because it is empty, it destroys all the theories of attachment held by ordinary people and all the theories of views held by non-Buddhists;

Because it is provisional (*prajñapti*), it refutes the minor substantiality of the three baskets and four gates, and refutes the minor substantiality common to the views of the three types of people;

because it is the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), it refutes the partial substantiality of the gradual [path], such that there are no longer the dharmas of the four truths as causes and effects involving various inversions, minor biases, and so forth, nor are there even the names of the Three Jewels (*triratna*) as minor or biased entities. There exists only the reality-mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of cause and effect, wherein the four truths and the Three Jewels are perfectly and fully present.
It also possesses all skillful means, causes and effects, the Four Noble Truths, and the Three Jewels.
Why is this? Because the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the ocean of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); these three truths alone constitute the true mark.
Furthermore, the unfolding of the reality of the sequential stages is itself the perfect reality, for the realization of the Way is identical in all cases.
Moreover, the unfolding of the reality attained in common by the three types of persons is such that, through profound inquiry, one reaches the ultimate limit.
Furthermore, it reveals the reality of the Tripiṭaka and definitively resolves the teachings for śrāvakas.
Moreover, it reveals the reality of various philosophical views; by remaining unmoved by such views, one cultivates the factors of enlightenment.

Furthermore, by revealing the reality of all discourses on desire, one realizes that the realm of Māra is itself the realm of the Buddha; thus, by traversing what are not paths, one penetrates the path of the Buddha.
Within all phenomena, there is entirely the nature of peace and bliss.
That which is immediately free from dependence and reveals the reality is the essence of this sutra.

Fifth, regarding the analysis by means of parables: I shall now borrow three metaphors to correctly manifest the distinction between the false and the true, while simultaneously clarifying the intent behind the principles of opening and closing, as well as refutation and reconciliation.

First, it is like the parable of three animals crossing a river: they all enter the water together, yet the three animals differ in strength, and the river has a bottom and banks. The rabbit and the horse are weak; though they reach the opposite shore, they float shallowly and do not go deep, nor do they reach the bottom.
The elephant is strong; it reaches both the bottom and the banks.

The metaphor of the three animals represents three types of persons; the water represents emptiness (*śūnyatā*), while the bottom represents non-emptiness. The wisdom of the two vehicles is shallow and unable to seek deeply, which is likened to the rabbit and the horse;
the wisdom of the Bodhisattvas is profound, which is likened to the great elephant.
The softness of the water represents emptiness; they all perceive emptiness equally, yet do not perceive non-emptiness.
The "bottom" is a metaphor for the true reality (*dharmatā*). The Bodhisattva alone reaches it; the wise one perceives both emptiness and non-emptiness.
There are two ways of reaching it:

a small elephant merely reaches the mud at the bottom, whereas a great elephant reaches deep down to the solid earth. Discriminative wisdom, though it perceives non-emptiness, does so through successive distinctions rather than as the ultimate reality. Perfect vision perceives non-emptiness and fully reveals the truth.

This analogy not only excludes and refutes the two vehicles of the rabbit and the horse as being unreal, but also excludes the small elephant as being non-empty yet unreal; rather, it takes the great elephant as non-empty to be the essence of this sutra.
This is a distinction made by taking emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*) together as the True Truth (*satyārtha*).

Second, it is like the comparison between the crystal and the wish-fulfilling gem: although the two jewels are similar and their forms and characteristics appear identical, the crystal is merely empty and cannot rain down treasures.
The wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi) is both empty and rains down jewels.
Crystal, which lacks jewels, serves as a metaphor for biased emptiness;

the wish-fulfilling jewel’s ability to rain down [jewels] serves as a metaphor for the Middle Way. These are combined as the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) in terms of existence and non-existence, distinguishing the false to reveal the true.
Now, the essence of this sutra is the same as that of the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*).
Furthermore, if one were to employ only a single wish-fulfilling gem as a metaphor, it would be like obtaining the gem without knowing its power and function—it would be merely the gem itself.
When the wise attain it, they gain much;
when those of the Two Vehicles attain emptiness, they realize emptiness and find rest;
when Bodhisattvas attain emptiness, they employ skillful means for the benefit of others, universally delivering all beings.
This is based on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) within the conventional realm, distinguishing between what is attained and what is lost.
Now, as for this sutra, it is like a wise person who obtains a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*), taking it as the essence of the sutra.
Third, it is like gold within yellow ore: a foolish person, lacking discernment, looks at it and calls it stone; they cast it away among filth and refuse, paying it no heed whatsoever.
When a merchant obtains it, he simply extracts the gold from it and treasures it;
when a goldsmith obtains it, he fashions it into various hairpins, bracelets, rings, and pots;
when an immortal obtains it, he refines it into elixir gold, flying through the heavens and entering the earth, reaching out to touch the sun and moon, transforming and acting with sovereign ease.
The "rustic" (yárén) is a metaphor for all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); though they possess the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), they do not know how to cultivate it.

The "merchant" (gùkè) is a metaphor for those of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*); they merely sever the ore of afflictions (*kleśa*) and preserve the gold of emptiness, having nothing further to do.

The analogy of the goldsmith represents the Bodhisattva of the Distinct Teaching (biejiao), who employs skillful means to know that emptiness is not [mere] emptiness; he emerges into the provisional realm to transform sentient beings, adorning the Buddha-lands and bringing sentient beings to fulfillment.

The "Immortal Guest" is a metaphor for the Bodhisattva of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). In accordance with phenomena yet identical to the Truth, at the very moment of first generating the resolve for enlightenment, he attains perfect awakening; he obtains a single body that is simultaneously infinite bodies, universally responding to all beings.
Now, this sutra takes only the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the golden elixir as its essential substance.
To employ a metaphor based on their commonality: from beginning to end, it is all gold; likewise, both the ordinary person and the Perfect Teaching are equally the true reality.
To provide an analogy based on difference: first, the stone differs from the gold; next, the gold differs from the vessel;

and the vessel differs from the vermilion. The color of the vermilion is pure and transparent, resembling clear oil; it is soft, supple, and exquisite—how could it be the same as the ring or the bracelet? Their forms diverge and their colors differ; therefore, they are not of one kind.
This is an analysis of gain and loss through the method of granting and withholding.
These three metaphors are cited to distinguish between these outcomes: the first metaphor concerns the nature of the faculties (*indriya*).

Since the nature of the faculties has varying degrees of depth—whether shallow, deep, or intermediate—one may, depending on the level, realize emptiness, realize the provisional, or realize the Middle Way.
Next, there are three types of sentient beings:
first, those who merely emerge from suffering but do not aspire to seek the Buddha-way, ceasing their practice upon seeing the Truth.
Second, those whose dispositions are fragmented and thus cannot cultivate the path in its entirety.
The latter seeks extensively throughout the entire dharma-realm.
Third, there is an analogy for the three types of skillful means:
the skillful means of the two vehicles are meager, like remaining while guarding gold;
The skillful means of the Separate Teaching (biejiao) are weak, being able only to adorn and manage one's livelihood;
the skillful means of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) are profound, thus able to swallow the clouds and encompass the Milky Way.

Now, to clarify the essence of the true reality (shixiang) of this sutra: it is like a great elephant reaching the bottom [of a deep pool], firm and indestructible, used as a metaphor for the wondrousness of its essence.
The universal rain of perfect pearls illustrates the subtlety of its function;
the attainment of immortality through skillful wisdom illustrates the subtlety of its essence.
These three analogies correspond to the three virtues (*triguṇa*); their being neither vertical nor horizontal is what is called the Mahāyāna.
Within the Mahāyāna, the true nature (*tathatā*) is specifically designated as the essence of the sūtra.

Sixth, regarding the distinction based on realization: if the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are truly as described above, yet one’s practice has not yet conformed to this principle, how can it be called "Truth" (*satya*)?

To labor in vain with these four descriptions is to pursue awakening while generating delusion; hearing of "powder" they say it is soft, hearing of "snow" they say it is cold, hearing of "conch shell" they say it is hard, and hearing of "crane" they say it is moving, yet in the end they cannot perceive the true color of the milk.
Wandering at night in the darkness of passion, how could one reach the Truth?
Crying out in search of food, there is no possibility of satiety.
Clinging to oneself as real, one holds all else to be false speech.
"This exists" and "that does not exist"—as these affirmations and negations arise alternately, they further increase the flux of the mind; how, then, can this be called the Truth (*satya*)?

If you wish to perceive the Truth, you must possess a sense of shame and modesty, repent with utmost sincerity, and move the Buddhas through such resonance. Thus, meditative concentration and wisdom will be awakened, the observing mind will become luminous and pure, and your faith and understanding will become empty and harmonious.
At that time, it is still like seeing a stump in the dark; the vision is hazy and indistinct, and one cannot yet clearly distinguish between a person, a tree, an insect, or dust.

If one can practice patient endurance (*kṣānti*) so that no craving for the Dharma arises, ignorance will be shattered and cleared away. Like a motionless bright mirror or still water without ripples, the forms of fish and stones appear spontaneously and naturally. When the pure mind is ever-unified, such a noble and sublime person is then able to see Prajñā; like using a golden surgical probe to clear the eyes, one sees distinctly with one finger, two fingers, and three fingers.
At that time, when perceiving a form, to say it exists is correct, and to say it does not exist is also correct.
Why is it said to exist?
Because it is a truly real form corresponding to the eye; because its principle accords with wisdom—this is what is called "existence."
What is meant by "non-existence"?
It is called non-existence when the characteristics of solidity, coldness, softness, and motion no longer exist.
The Treatise says:
All is real, all is unreal, all is both real and unreal, and all is neither real nor unreal.
These are called the true marks of all dharmas.
Just as Śāriputra, abiding in true wisdom, [thought]:
"I shall certainly become a Buddha, revered by devas and humans.
Only at that time can it be said that [defilements] are forever extinguished without remainder; this is called the essence of true vision.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"The eight thousand śrāvakas, having perceived the Tathāgata-nature within the *Lotus Sūtra*, are like those who have finished harvesting in autumn and storing for winter; there is nothing further to be done."
To clarify "non-action" (akṛtaka) in terms of principle: this is the ultimate principle.
To clarify "non-action" in terms of teaching: having heard this teaching, one hears nothing further from elsewhere.
Regarding "acting in accordance with practice without anything to be done": having cultivated this practice, one no longer alters the course.
Such are the various meanings of "non-action," and so forth.
To speak briefly, by attaining wondrous awakening through wisdom, one perceives the essence of the sutra.

One should employ the mind of wondrous awakening that accords with wisdom; as one traverses the various realms of the Truths (satya), there are at each stage various distinctions between that which accords with emotion, that which accords with wisdom, and that which accords with both emotion and wisdom. By eliminating other emotional conceptions and taking only that which accords with wisdom, one clearly perceives the essence of the Sūtra.
III. Regarding the different names for a single dharma, there are further four sections:
first, the presentation of the different names;
second, the explanation.
3. Illustration by analogy.
4. Analysis according to the four followings.

First, regarding the presentation of alternative names: the essence of the true mark (*dharmatā*) is but a single dharma, yet the Buddha has spoken of it under various names, such as: wondrous existence (*prabhāsvara*), truly good and wondrous form, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), suchness (*tathatā*), nirvāṇa, the buddha-nature of space, the tathāgatagarbha, the mind of the central true principle, the middle way that is neither existent nor non-existent, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and subtle, wondrous quiescence, among others.
The countless different names are all alternative designations for the true nature (bhūtalakṣaṇa), and the true nature itself is merely another designation for these various names.
Those who are deluded remain stuck in confusion, clinging to the names and interpreting them as distinct.
The Sūtra states:
"Those who lack wisdom and harbor doubt and regret shall suffer eternal loss.

The masters of the Hīnayāna treatises focus exclusively on names and characteristics to give rise to disputes and contention; they disparage the Dharma and vilify others, with each successive generation imitating their ways, thereby becoming enemies of the Dharma.

It is the same for those who study the Mahāyāna: those who study the "wondrous existence" (prabhāsvara-bhāva) claim it to be the ultimate, yet upon hearing of "ultimate emptiness" (atyanta-śūnyatā), they give rise to slander, refusing to accept that teaching and finding no patience for its proponents;
while those who study ultimate emptiness gather in like-minded circles, drawing the correct toward themselves and casting what is erroneous onto others.

None of them knew the thousand names of the Lord of Devas; upon hearing "Śakra Devānām Indra," they rejoiced, but upon hearing "husband of Śacī," they were angered. They venerated Diśi while showing contempt for Kauśika; thus, it was feared that their merit would not compensate for their transgression.
The true nature (*dharmatā*) is likewise so; since it is one and the same Dharma, how could one possibly slander one while believing in another?
Second, regarding the explanation: the names and entities of the Hīnayāna have been easy to understand from the outset, so they shall be set aside and not discussed here.
The distinctions made here concern only the separate (bie) and perfect (yuan) teachings across eight gates.
These are further categorized into four propositions:
first, where name, meaning, and substance are identical.
2. The name and the referent differ while the substance is the same;
3. the name and the referent are the same while the substance differs;
4. the name and the referent differ while the substance is the same.
Regarding the first phrase: "wondrous existence" (miao-you) is its name; "true, good, and wondrous form" (zhen-shan-miao-se) is its meaning; and "the limit of reality" (ji-ji) is its essence.
Next, "ultimate emptiness" (bi-jing-kong) is its name; "suchness" (ru-ru) is its meaning; and "nirvana" (nie-pan) is its essence.
Next, it is named "Buddha-nature of Space" (*ākāśa-buddhadhātu*), with "Tathāgatagarbha" as its meaning and "the mind of the central, substantial principle" as its essence.
Next, it is named "the Middle Way that is neither existent nor non-existent," with "the Ultimate Truth" (*paramārtha-satya*) as its meaning and "subtle, wondrous quiescence" as its essence.

Regarding such names as these, although their underlying principles differ, they all employ a single gateway; since their intent is not distinct, it is said that their names, meanings, and essences are identical.

Regarding the second phrase, "the name, meaning, and essence are distinct": for example, "wondrous existence" (*adbhuta-bhāva*) is the name, "ultimate emptiness" (*atyanta-śūnyatā*) is the meaning, and the *tathāgatagarbha* is the essence.
Furthermore, "emptiness" is the name, the *tathāgatagarbha* is the meaning, and the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*) is the essence.
Furthermore, "Tathāgatagarbha" is the name, the Middle Way is the meaning, and wondrous existence (*prabhāsvara-bhāva*) is the essence.
Moreover, the "Middle Way" is the name, "wondrous existence" is the meaning, and emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the essence.
In this way, these four categories differ from one another; since the three aspects are all distinct, it is said that "name, meaning, and substance are different.

Regarding the third category, where "name and meaning are the same while the substance is different": for example, taking "wondrous existence" as the name, "wondrous form" as the meaning, and "ultimate emptiness" as the substance. Thus, two are identical while one is distinct; therefore, it is said that "name and meaning are the same while the substance is different."
Furthermore, "emptiness" is the name, "suchness" is the meaning, and "wondrous existence" is the essence; here too, two are identical while one is distinct.
The same applies to the other two gates; therefore, it is said that the names and meanings are identical while the essences differ.

The fourth phrase, "names and meanings differ while the substance is the same," refers to such terms as "wondrous existence" (*miaoyou*) and so forth. While the names differ from one another—such as "true," "good," and "form" (*rūpa*), whose respective meanings are distinct—they all ultimately converge into a single essence without any further bifurcation; therefore, it is said that "names and meanings differ while the substance is the same."
The three gates are likewise.

In the first three phrases, both name and meaning are not yet integrated; the first phrase seeks one name, attains one meaning, and attains one essence, being perfectly integrated within its own gate without regard for other matters.
The second phrase seeks alternative names, identifying differences in meaning and essence; since essence, meaning, and name are least harmonious here, this is easy to understand.

In the third phrase, since the essence is not harmonious, although the name and meaning are the same, they ultimately remain incompatible; these are all distinct sections clarifying specific meanings.
Those who do not grasp the intended meaning give rise to disputes from this: either the small [vehicle] encroaches upon the great, or the great seizes from the small. Why is this?

Those of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) wish to sever birth and death; when they hear that it is ultimately not merely emptiness, they follow their own inclinations and claim it is merely emptiness, clinging to this and giving rise to dispute.
Furthermore, because the followers of the Hīnayāna desire to sever birth and death, they do not hold that [reality] exists;
yet, because they refute the affliction of clinging to nirvāṇa, they do not hold that it does not exist.

Upon hearing of the Middle Way as being neither existent nor non-existent, they bolster their own limited inclinations by claiming that this "neither existent nor non-existent" is their own scripture. Consequently, they frequently give rise to disputes and contention regarding these two gates.
If one hears the true principle of the Middle Way and the mind accords with it while diverging from the minor characteristics, then no dispute will arise. Why?

Because the followers of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) habitually dwell in emptiness, whereas here they hear of existence; the Two Vehicles seek to extinguish the body and annihilate wisdom, whereas here they hear of the wisdom-mind. Since this accords with their own [ultimate] intent, they do not cling to it or engage in dispute.
For this reason, the small [vehicle] encroaches upon the great and thus they contend.

When the great seizes from the small, those who study the Mahāyāna see that the practitioners of the three vehicles share the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*)—a gate that is neither empty nor existent—and yet, because its name is the same as that of the two vehicles, they fail to perceive its profound meaning; they consequently dismiss it as belonging to the characteristics of deception rather than the true school.

If one simply adopts the two gates of "wondrous existence" and "both emptiness and existence," thereby citing this doctrine of perfect permanence, then whether these two [gates] are transmitted or not transmitted, such a dispute may be considered somewhat acceptable.

If one understands that emptiness is not merely neither existent nor non-existent, but rather negates both extremes, then all four positions are simultaneously refuted; yet, regarding the minor suffering, there remains contention over two positions.

Furthermore, regarding the four gates of the Mahāyāna, their names and meanings are not harmonized; each gate disputes the others, devouring one another. How much more so for you followers of the Hīnayāna—like jackals usurping the lion’s domain—how could they not devour you?
The first three phrases give rise to dispute; they do not constitute the essence of this sutra.
The fourth phrase refers to a difference in name and meaning while identity of essence; since the essence possesses manifold meanings, its functional utility is exceedingly great.

The four gates follow conditions and possess various different names; because their essence is harmonious, they respond perfectly to all appellations. Since the substance of the Dharma is identical, there is no contention over these differing names and meanings.
What are its characteristics?
I shall now briefly explain them.
The *Anantamukha-sūtra* (*Wuliangyi jing*) says:
"The meaning of 'immeasurable' arises from a single dharma.
This single dharma is what is called the true aspect (bhūtalakṣaṇa).

As for the aspect of the true aspect: it is neither having an aspect nor not having an aspect; it is neither non-aspect nor aspect. This is named the true aspect, which derives its name from being indestructible and ultimate reality."
Furthermore, because the Buddhas have realized this true mark (dharmatā), it is called "wondrous existence" (pranīta-bhāva).
Although this wondrous existence cannot be seen by others, the Buddhas are able to see it; therefore, it is called "true, good, and wondrous form" (bhūta-kuśala-praṇīta-rūpa).
The true mark (*dharmatā*) is not the existence of the two extremes; therefore, it is called ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).
The principle of emptiness is serene and profound, being neither one nor different; therefore, it is called suchness (*tathatā*).
The true mark is quiescent and extinguished; therefore, it is called nirvāṇa.
Awakened awareness that remains unchanging is therefore called the *ākāśa-buddhadhātu* (space-Buddha-nature).
Because it contains and receives all things, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha* (Tathāgata-womb).
Because it is quiescent illumination and numinous cognition, it is called the mind of the central, substantial principle.
It does not rely on existence, nor does it adhere to non-existence;
therefore, it is called the Middle Way. It is unsurpassed and supreme; therefore, it is called the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Such various different names all refer to the True Aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). The various reasons for these names are all the functional capacities of the True Aspect. Since its essence is perfect, there is no separation between name and meaning; this is indeed the fundamental substance of the sutra.
Furthermore, since all phenomena (*dharmas*) are alternative names for the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), the true nature is the very essence of those phenomena;
and since the true nature is also an alternative name for all phenomena, all phenomena are the very essence of that true nature.
The wondrous existence is indestructible, and is therefore called the "true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Because the Buddhas are able to perceive it, it is called "truly good and wondrous form.
Because it is not mixed with other things, it is called "ultimate emptiness" (*atyantaśūnyatā*).
Being non-dual and without distinction, it is called *tathatā* (suchness).
Being awakened and unchanging, it is called *buddhadhātu* (Buddha-nature).
Containing and encompassing all dharmas, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha* (Tathāgata-store).
Quiescent yet luminously aware, it is therefore called the "mind of the central reality-principle.
It excludes and transcends all extremes, and is thus termed the "Middle Way.
Being unsurpassed and faultless, it is named the "Ultimate Truth" (*paramārtha-satya*).
One may establish a designation based on any given phenomenon according to its essential nature or its function; other cases can be understood by analogy with this.
As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states:
"The dharma of liberation has many names; though there are a hundred phrases for liberation, they are all but a single liberation."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"If one contemplates the Buddha in accordance with the Dharma, then Prajñā, Nirvāṇa, and the Buddha—these three are of one single characteristic; in reality, there is no difference between them."
If one attains this meaning, one knows that all various names are called the true mark (lakṣaṇa), and are also called prajñā, and also called liberation (vimukti).
These three dharmas are the names for all dharmas, and all dharmas are the substance of these three dharmas, and so forth.
Third, the illustration by analogy: For example, there is a man named Goldsmith who is able to forge gold; its substance is yellow, which illustrates the dharma of the first phrase.
Again, for example, there is a man named Blue who is able to produce lacquer, yet his own body is pure white.
Furthermore, there is one person named "Crow" who is able to grind cinnabar, and his body becomes purple.
There are countless hundreds of thousands such as these, whose names and physical forms differ; this is analogous to the second phrase.
For example, suppose there are one hundred people who share the same surname, the same name, and the same proficiency in a single craft, yet each has a distinct body; this is like the third case.

Or, for example, suppose a single person encounters family calamities during times of turmoil and changes their surname in various places and alters their name in various places—such as Zhang Yi or Fan Li—who hold many official posts and occupy numerous positions throughout their life.
If named after their many skills, they are masters of calligraphy, painting, metallurgy, and so forth;
if named after civil offices, they are scholars of the Confucian tradition or Secretaries of the Palace;
if named after military offices, they are Xiongqu or Cifei.
Changing names according to different locations illustrates the difference in names;
receiving titles according to one's skills illustrates the difference in meanings;
yet the essence is one and the same, being no different person.
The Sūtra states:

"A royal wrestler can match a thousand. This man does not necessarily possess strength equal to a thousand; rather, he is called a "match-for-a-thousand" because his various skills enable him to overcome a thousand.
He is skilled in all arts, such that there is no craft he does not master; he has served in all ranks, such that there is no office he has not held.

He is an indestructible person, a person of wondrous skill, a person of vital spirit, and a person free from faults and afflictions. He is a person of universal penetration who can defeat enemies, a person of noble lineage, a person rich in wealth and talent, a person of great knowledge, a person of integrity and honesty among the common people, and a person who serves as a protective canopy—comparable, for example, to the fourth line of a verse.
The analogy makes it clear; therefore, we know that the first three phrases belong to the distinct (vyatireka) meaning, while the final phrase belongs to the perfect (pariniṣpanna) meaning.
Fourth, regarding the four types of conformity (catur-anuvartana):
Question:
The reality of phenomena is a single dharma; why, then, are its names and meanings so diverse?
Answer:
In accordance with the capacities of those beings, there are various distinctions, responding to their inclinations, their suitability, their needs for treatment, and their need for awakening.

For example, among worldly people, those who study the Numerical Discourses (Āgama) abandon the Great [Vehicle]; those who practice the Vaipulya discard the Small; those who habituate themselves to emptiness loathe existence; and those who take pleasure in the Stages (Bhūmi) disparage the Middle Way.

Since they do not wish to hear these teachings, they find no joy in hearing them; lacking the intent to believe and accept them, they do not extinguish their afflictions, nor do they give rise to the mind of enlightenment.
Each had become habituated through exclusive study of their own scriptures, which served as the causal conditions for becoming roots capable of hearing the Dharma in the future.

At that time, the Tathāgata, observing their faculties such as faith with his Buddha-eye, preached the Dharma to them using various words and phrases according to their respective capacities and expedient means.

For those of a root-nature for existence, one preaches the wondrous existence and the truly good, wondrous form; this is neither contradictory nor contrary [to their disposition]. Through faith, precepts, patience, and diligence, they sweep away views of emptiness and are thus able to awaken and enter, attuning themselves to the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

For those of empty root-nature, he teaches ultimate emptiness, suchness, nirvana, and so forth; listen attentively and receive this with earnestness, using the good to overcome the evil—the signless is supreme.

For those who [perceive] both emptiness and the nature of the faculties, I speak of the Buddha-nature of empty space, the Tathāgatagarbha, and the mind of the true reality within; they joyfully give rise to goodness and depart from impurity by abandoning non-mind.

For those whose spiritual capacity is neither that of emptiness nor that of existence, one teaches the Middle Way that is neither existent nor non-existent, which excludes the two extremes, and is characterized by neither coming nor going, neither annihilation nor permanence, and neither identity nor difference.

Desiring to hear and listen, one rejoices as if drinking to quench thirst; through faithful joy and cultivation, all manner of goodness arises, all erroneous views are dispelled, and no evil remains unexhausted, so that the ultimate principle suddenly dawns with clarity.

Following these four faculties, there are four different expositions through four gates; they are called "different" because their explanations differ, and their meanings differ because their functions are distinct, yet the realization of the principle is not diverse, for their essence is ultimately one.
Thus, Guṇavarman said:

"The various treatises differ in their approaches, yet the principle of practice is non-dual; those who cling to partiality find right and wrong, but the one who has attained realization has no conflict."
Therefore, the four [teachings] are merely different expressions of the One Reality.

○ Fourth, clarifying the gateway for entering the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*): Now, the true mark is profound and subtle, its principle deep and abstruse; just as one ascending a precipice must rely on a flying ladder, so too, to accord with the true source, one must depend upon teaching and practice. Thus, teaching and practice constitute the gateway.
The subsequent text states:
"By means of the gateway of the Buddha's teaching, one emerges from the suffering of the triple world.
Once the Son of the Buddha has practiced the Way, he shall attain Buddhahood in a future life."
This refers to what is called the "Gate of Capable Penetration.
Briefly stated, there are four points:
first, a brief indication of the characteristics of the gate.
2. Showing the contemplation for entering the gate;
3. Showing the coarse and the subtle;
4. Showing the revelation and clarification.

Regarding the manifestation of the characteristics of the gateway: the Buddha-dharma is inherently inexpressible; yet, when teaching in accordance with conditions, one must necessarily employ the four propositions to elucidate the principle, thereby enabling practitioners to penetrate the ground of reality.
The *Mahā-śāstra* states:

"Regarding such dharmas, the ultimate standpoint (*paramārtha-siddhānta*) is taught as follows: namely, that all is real, all is unreal, all is both real and unreal, and all is neither real nor unreal."
"All such things are called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all dharmas.
Since even the true mark is not a single entity, how could one speak of four?
One should know that these four are merely 'gateways for entering the true mark.'"
It is further said:
"Entering the Cool Lake through the four gates"—these gates are unobstructed; it is not only those who are sharp-witted who may enter, but even those who are dull-witted may enter as well.
It is not only those in meditative concentration who may enter, but even those with distracted minds, those who are single-mindedly focused, and those who are diligent may also enter.
Furthermore, it is said:
"Prajñā has four kinds of characteristics, namely: the characteristic of existence, the characteristic of non-existence, and even the characteristic of neither existence nor non-existence.
If Prajñā is not even a single characteristic, how can there be four?
One should know that this, too, is an entrance into the gate of Prajñā.
It is further said:
"The Prajñāpāramitā is like a great mass of flames; it cannot be grasped from any of its four sides because it is consumed by the fire of false views."
"If one does not touch fire, it warms the body and ripens food;
if one touches fire, the fire burns the body.
Once the body is burned, warming food is useless."
The four gates fundamentally lead to Prajñāpāramitā, eliminating afflictions and accomplishing the great task.
If one grasps at them with attachment, they become false views and burn the Dharma-body.
Since the Dharma-body has already been incinerated, through what do the four gates pass?
If they do not touch the fire, the gates can pass.
If one takes the Buddha’s teaching as the gate, the teaching is briefly summarized into four [categories], and so forth.
If, within a single teaching, the principle is elucidated through four propositions, these constitute four gates; four sets of four combined result in sixteen gates.
If one takes practice as the gate, then by receiving the teaching and cultivating contemplation, entering through the power of reflection constitutes taking practice as the gate.
If one awakens to the truth by means of the teachings, then the teachings serve as the gateway.
If, upon first hearing the teachings, one is like a swift horse that enters the correct path at the mere sight of the whip’s shadow, there is no need for further cultivation of contemplation.
If, when first practicing contemplation, one attains the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga) like seeing a flash of lightning at night, no further instruction is required.
This is entirely due to the ripening of roots of goodness from the past; having attained penetration now through the gateway of teaching, one is called a "Faith-follower" (śraddhānusārin);
having attained penetration through the gateway of contemplation, one is called a "Dharma-follower" (dharmānusārin).
If one hears [the teaching] but does not immediately awaken to it, one must practice contemplation;
for those who awaken through contemplation, it is transformed into the practice of the Dharma (dharmacaryā).
If one practices contemplation but does not awaken, one must once again listen to the Dharma.
Upon hearing the Dharma and attaining awakening, one changes the name to "Faith-Practice" (śraddhācaryā).
Teaching itself constitutes the gate of contemplation (vipaśyanā), and contemplation itself constitutes the gate of teaching (śruta).
Hearing the teaching while contemplating, and contemplating the teaching while hearing—when teaching and contemplation support one another—one enters through the gate of accomplishment.
If one were to synthesize the teachings and contemplations into a treatise, there would be thirty-two gates; this number merely refers to the general count.
If one examines these gates in detail, they are in fact immeasurable.

Regarding the causes for five hundred bodies, the thirty-two gates of non-duality, Sudhana’s journey through the Dharma-realm, his encounters with immeasurable spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), and the immeasurable teaching-gates and immeasurable contemplative practices he encountered—these are all included therein.
Just as the city of Sudarśana has one thousand two hundred gates, how could the city of the Dharma of the true mark have but a single path?
As a sutra says:
"By expounding various Dharma-gates, he proclaims and reveals the Buddha-way."
Now, for the time being, we shall clarify the characteristics of the sixteen gates according to the four teachings.
Regarding the four gates of the Tripitaka:

first is the gate of existence (*yōmon*). This refers to the phenomena of birth and death, which are fundamentally not created by a primal nature (*seishō*), atoms (*mikujin*), or parents; rather, they are produced through the causal conditions of ignorance (*mumyō*) as the primary cause, giving rise to the various formations (*gyō*), afflictions (*bonnō*), karma (*gō*), and suffering (*ku*). Thus, the three paths (*sandō*) are all entirely existent.

All conditioned phenomena are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; they can give rise to the stages of Heat, Summits, and the Supreme Worldly Dharmas, producing the true cause for outflow-free wisdom, and employing the true path of cultivation.
This is the Truth of the Path, which also exists.
Once the seeds and fruits [of affliction] are severed, one attains the nirvana with remainder and the nirvana without remainder.
Thus, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* says:
"The profound principle is ineffable; in the ultimate reality, there are no sounds or letters. Yet, the bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya has attained true knowledge and vision regarding all phenomena."
This means that through the cessation of causes, one realizes the Truth (tattva), yet this Truth is also a form of existence.
This is what is set forth in the various Abhidharma treatises: the view that one attains the Path by perceiving existence; this is the "Gate of Existence" (yōmon).

Second, as for the Gate of Emptiness (*śūnyatā-mukha*): it refers to the analysis within that teaching of the primary causes and conditions—ignorance (*avidyā*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), the two truths of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*)—as being insubstantial and illusory. By destroying the distinction between the provisional and the real, all enter into the equality of emptiness. One awakens to the true, untainted state (*anāsrava*); by means of emptiness one perceives the Truth, and thus emptiness is the gate to the Ultimate Meaning (*paramārtha*).
Therefore, Subhūti stayed in a stone chamber, contemplating birth and cessation, impermanence, and entering into emptiness.
Through emptiness he attained the Way and beheld the Buddha’s Dharma-body; it is feared that this is what is expounded in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.
Third, regarding the gates of existence and emptiness: this refers to that teaching which clarifies that the arising and ceasing of the correct causes and conditions are both existent and empty.

If one receives this teaching, one can break through biased attachments to existence and non-existence, seeing that within dependent origination there is both existence and emptiness, thereby giving rise to true outflow-free wisdom. Because one perceives the truth through the views of existence and non-existence, existence and non-existence themselves constitute the gate to the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*).
This was the gateway through which Kātyāyana entered the Path; therefore, he composed the *Kuṇālā-śāstra* (or *Kun-le lun*) to further expound this very gateway.

Fourth, the gateway of "neither existence nor non-existence" refers to the principle of neither existence nor non-existence as clarified in that teaching regarding the arising and ceasing of true causes and conditions.

If one receives this teaching, one can shatter the boundless false attachments to existence and non-existence, seeing that causes and conditions are neither existent nor non-existent. One gives rise to true outflow-free wisdom by perceiving reality through the view that they are neither existent nor non-existent; thus, being neither existent nor non-existent is the gateway to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The wicked-mouthed Chanda entered the Way because of this, though no treatise on the matter has yet appeared.

Some say that the *Vātsīputrīya Abhidharma* expresses this intent; that treatise clarifies that the self exists within the fifth "inexpressible basket" (*avyākṛta-piṭaka*). Because the self is not of the three periods of time, it is not a "self";
because it is not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is not a "non-self."
This [previous analysis] likely cannot yet be definitively applied.

Second, regarding the characteristics of the four gates of the Shared Teaching (Sādhāraṇa-yāna): these are Mahāyāna gates that encompass both the universal and the particular; they must not be grasped in a one-sided manner.

Now, to discuss the four gates by way of general principles: the four gates of the aforementioned Tripiṭaka all involve the cessation of form to enter emptiness; for example, when one analyzes a real person into six parts, such as the head and so forth, and fails to find a person, it is therefore called "emptiness."

In the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), all four gates maintain that form is itself emptiness; as when observing a reflected image, its six parts are themselves empty without waiting for them to be analytically dismantled until nothing remains.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The Buddha told the bhikṣus:"
"To contemplate emptiness is to see the cloth; to contemplate the cloth is to see emptiness.
This refers to the gate of essence (tǐmén) as distinct from the gate of analysis (xīmén).

In the Tripiṭaka [teaching], one attains the Way by contemplating the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā); having attained the Way through contemplating the emptiness of persons, one further contemplates the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā), yet the two objects—persons and phenomena—are not integrated.

Now, according to the general gate, the emptiness of sentient beings is identical to the emptiness of dharmas, and the emptiness of dharmas is identical to the emptiness of sentient beings; they are non-dual and without distinction.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
"The nature of form is like the nature of the self, and the nature of the self is like the nature of form; both of these are like illusions and transformations."
Some say: The Tripiṭaka refutes the calculation of a real nature; by investigating dharmas as real entities, one finds no self, which is merely observing the emptiness of nature.
The Mahāyāna clarifies that the self-nature of marks is itself empty; there is no need to investigate them further to establish their emptiness.
This is merely a preliminary statement.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:

"The nature of all things is eternally empty; there is no time when they are not empty by nature. To clearly understand all phenomena as being like illusions, transformations, the moon reflected in water, or images in a mirror—how could this be limited to the emptiness of mere characteristics!
Based solely on this illusory transformation, the four gates are distinguished.
The Treatise states:
"All is real; all is unreal; all is both real and unreal; all is neither real nor unreal."
Regarding these four lines, the Buddha extensively expounds the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate standpoint).
As for "all things being real" as a provisional gate: whether it be karma or its fruit, phenomena such as good and evil, or even *nirvāṇa*, they are all like illusions and transformations.
It is like an image in a mirror: although it lacks substantial reality, it possesses the six parts such as the illusory head and so forth; this constitutes the gate of existence (*yǒumén*).

Since all phenomena are like illusions and transformations, and illusions and transformations are fundamentally without reality, they are empty because they lack reality. This extends even to *nirvāṇa*, which is like an image in a mirror—having a provisional form and color that cannot be found when sought; this is the gate of emptiness (*kōngmén*).
Since all phenomena are like illusions, they are called "existent.
Since illusions cannot be apprehended, they are called "empty.
Like a reflection in a mirror, which is seen yet not seen, and not seen yet seen—this is both the gate of emptiness and the gate of existence.
If even illusory existence cannot be apprehended, how much less can illusory emptiness be apprehended?
This is the gate of relinquishing both;
it is the four gates of "immediate emptiness" (sudden emptiness) in the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).

If those who receive the teachings of the three vehicles differ in their faculties and dispositions, each enters the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) through one of these four propositions; therefore, all four are called "gates.
Thus, Qingmu’s commentary on the treatise states:
"The true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena has three kinds."
Now, these people of the three vehicles enter this gate together; those who perceive the primary truth (paramārtha) do so through this single aspect of emptiness.
Third, regarding the explanation of the four gates of the Separate Teaching (pratyekavyavasthāna-naya):

if one uses the verse from the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, "It is also called a provisional designation," to distinguish the four gates, it is precisely as in the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which also carries the same meaning as these four propositions.
Regarding what is called "distinctive" (*bie*): it is distinct from the *Zang* (Tripitaka) and *Tong* (Shared) teachings below because it possesses seven meanings;
it is distinct from the Perfect Teaching (*Yuanjiao*) above because one enters the Middle Way through successive stages; thus, it is called "distinctive."

This intent is precisely derived from the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, though it is mostly presented in a scattered manner; now, by means of the analogies of milk and so forth, the four distinct gates are revealed.
The text states:
"Buddha-nature is like milk containing curd, gold within stone, and the jewel on the forehead of a strongman"—this is the gate of existence (*yǒumén*).
If the stone of Memyō (Meishaku) lacked the nature of gold, or if milk lacked the nature of curd, then the Buddha-nature of sentient beings would be like empty space.
The emptiness of the Great Parinirvāṇa and the emptiness of the city of Kapilavastu constitute the gate of emptiness.
Furthermore, it is said:
"Buddha-nature both exists and does not exist.
In what sense does it exist?
Since all sentient beings possess it entirely,
how can it be said that they do not?
It is because they perceive it through skillful means.
Furthermore, it is like milk, which both possesses the nature of curd and lacks the nature of curd; this is the gate of "both existing and non-existing.
If one clarifies that Buddha-nature is the Middle Way, it is the simultaneous negation of both extremes.
Furthermore, it is like milk, which neither possesses the nature of curd nor lacks the nature of curd; this is the gate of "neither empty nor existent.

Bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching (biejiao) receive these teachings of the four gates and, by perceiving their Buddha-nature, abide in Great Nirvana. Therefore, these four phrases constitute the four gates of the Distinct Teaching.

Superficially, this is intended as a parallel to the scriptural texts of the Separate Teaching (Bie-men), yet at times it serves the Perfect Teaching (Yuan-men); the details of this meaning will be clarified in the subsequent analysis.

Regarding the characteristics of the four gates of the Perfect Teaching, this gate clarifies entry into the Buddha-nature as the primary truth (paramārtha). While its names and meanings are, on the surface, identical to those of the Separate Teaching, upon careful investigation of their underlying intent, many distinct paths are revealed.
The detailed analysis of similarities and differences is discussed extensively below, as stated.
Second, the demonstration of the gateway to the contemplation is divided into two parts:
first, a brief indication of the entrance to the gateway.
2. A Brief Demonstration of the Contemplation for Entering the Gate.

Regarding the brief demonstration of the entry point: that which enables one to penetrate the gates of the teachings is broadly divided into sixteen sections; the principle thus penetrated consists solely of the two truths—the partial and the perfect. Of these, the first eight gates collectively enter the partial truth, while the latter eight gates collectively enter the perfect truth.
Why is it that there are eight gates for the single door of the True Truth alone?
The four gates of the Tripiṭaka are circuitous, narrow, and crude; they are called the "clumsy vehicle.
The four gates of the Shared Teaching belong to the Mahāyāna; they are broad, direct, and skillful.

There are distinctions between skillfulness and clumsiness regarding the gates, yet the capacity to penetrate them constitutes eight [paths]; the ultimate truth is non-dual, and that which is penetrated is but one.
It is like a provincial city with gates opened on four sides.
The side gates on the four sides are used as a metaphor for the Tripiṭaka;
the direct gates on the four sides are used as a metaphor for the Shared Teaching.
Since the side and direct gates differ, those capable of passing through them become eight, yet the lord who governs them is one, and that which is passed through is non-dual.
The four gates of the Separate Teaching (biejiao) are partial and not yet integrated;
the four gates of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) are perfect and fully integrated.
Since the partial and the perfect differ, that which enables penetration becomes eightfold; yet since the perfect and the true are non-dual, that which is penetrated is but one.

For example, it is like an imperial city with four main gates and four side gates; the side gates are used as a metaphor for the Separate Teaching (biejiao), while the four main gates are used as a metaphor for the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao).
Since the side and main gates differ, those capable of providing passage amount to eight; yet the imperial sovereign is non-dual, and that which is passed through is but one, and so forth.
Question:
The Hīnayāna has one type of fourfold gate; why does the Mahāyāna have three types of fourfold gates?
Answer:
The Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) is shallow and superficial; severing the fetters within a single lifetime is like a small household.

The Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) is profound and far-reaching; its scope is vast, like a great mansion that requires thousands of doors and ten thousand windows—how could three or four be considered many?
Question:
In the Mahāyāna vehicle, how can three types of persons realize the truth?
Answer:

The primary intent of this gate extends to the Mahāyāna, while its secondary application extends to the Hīnayāna. It is like a kingdom that has both general gates and private gates: a private gate provides access for court officials, whereas a general gate provides access to both the court and the marketplace; it cannot be said that the latter is a "gate for the common people" simply because the populace may tread upon it.

The gateway of the Mahāyāna is likewise: it penetrates directly into the true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa) and penetrates indirectly into the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya). Therefore, even the three vehicles' cessation of defilements (kṣaya-nirodha) are concurrently achieved through this gateway; it cannot be called a Hinayāna gateway merely because it also penetrates the limited truth (saṃvṛtisatya).

Second, a brief indication of the contemplation for entering the gate: first, we clarify the gate of existence (*yu-men*) within the Three Baskets (*piṭaka*). Within that gate of existence, there are those who possess faith in the Dharma and faith in practice; they attain awakening immediately upon hearing the teaching. Because their minds are swift and sharp, the methods for attaining the Way are difficult to demonstrate to others.
Furthermore, summarizing the practice of the gate of contemplation according to the Dharma, there are ten points:
first, identifying the object of contemplation;
second, truly generating the bodhicitta.
3. To practice concentration and wisdom;
4. To be able to shatter the pervasiveness of dharmas;
5. To skillfully know how to open what is obstructed.
Sixth, skillfully employing the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa).
Seventh, skillfully employing the remedies (pratipakṣa).
Eighth, skillfully knowing the stages and sequences.
Ninth, being well-able to practice patient endurance;
tenth, the non-arising of craving for the Dharma.

These ten points are fully contained within the Abhidharma, yet their textual expressions are scattered throughout. If a master of the treatises wishes to practice the Path, they will not know upon what to rely for cultivation; it would be like being confused at a fork in the road, unable to discern which way to follow.
Now, to summarize the essential meaning and provide a comprehensive overview from beginning to end, one recognizes that consciousness possesses the contemplation for entering the Way.
First, clarifying the object of contemplation: this refers to consciousness as the primary condition of ignorance, which gives rise to all phenomena.

If one claims that the phenomena of suffering and happiness in the world arise from Viṣṇu, or say they arise from primordial nature (prakṛti) or from atoms (paramāṇu), these are all produced by false causes and conditions.
If one says that things arise spontaneously and naturally (*dharmatā*) without any agent, this implies arising without causes and conditions.

To claim arising without causes and conditions is to negate the cause while failing to negate the effect; moreover, false causes and conditions likewise negate correct causes and effects. Such instances are not the domain of correct causes and conditions, and thus should not be objects of contemplation.
To maintain the existence of atoms while simultaneously refuting them in discourse is no different from heterodox views; it is surely not the realm of correct causes and conditions. Why is this?

Whether one asserts that atoms exist or do not exist, one cannot avoid the two [extreme] views; these remain the perversions of ignorance. Because they are perverted, they constitute "origination" (samudaya); because they are origination, they evoke coarse and subtle forms.
Since ignorance and its inversions are unreal, how can one definitively calculate whether the resulting fruit of suffering exists or not?
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Whether form is coarse or subtle, when observed as a whole, it is impermanent and without self."

Because there is no self, there is no master. Whether coarse or subtle, whether cause or condition, whether suffering or its origin, whether basis or path—all are impermanent and without a master; they are all produced by ignorance and inversion.

As explained extensively in the *Abhidharma-mukha*, this is called the object of observation for the correct causes and conditions of consciousness; it is not like the false, causeless [theories] of the non-Buddhists. Second, regarding the genuineness of the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*):

having recognized that ignorance, inversion, the formations, consciousness, and so forth up to old age and death, revolve like a whirling firebrand, one desires to bring rest to the fetters and karma, correctly seeking *nirvāṇa*. One arouses the mind of the Two Vehicles to transcend views and craving, without desiring fame or profit, but merely to destroy all modes of existence (*bhava*), not increasing suffering or its origin, and being solely intent upon the remainderless state. This mind is pure, unmixed, and without deceit; such a genuine mind is called "correctly arousing the mind," and it is not like that of the non-Buddhists or celestial Māras.

Third, regarding those who practice concentration and wisdom: once the practitioner has vowed to seek liberation and dwells in the cultivation of the path by relying on the *prātimokṣa*, yet their karmic obstacles remain turbulent and their mind finds no peace, how can the path be realized?
To cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), one studies the five objects of mental abiding (pañca-viṣaya-sthiti-citta) to destroy the five kinds of hindrances.

The contemplation of these five objects of abiding is concentration (samādhi); from concentration arises the foundations of mindfulness, which is wisdom (prajñā). When wisdom and concentration are balanced and stabilized, it is called "settling the mind" (anxin).
Furthermore, because concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are balanced and harmonized, it is called "settling the mind.
If one lacks both concentration and wisdom, or possesses only one of them, or if concentration and wisdom are not evenly balanced, one is not called a worthy person (*satpuruṣa*).

Just as the sages of the world are fully endowed with wisdom and virtue—wherein their wisdom is proficient in all things and their virtue is flawless in its beautiful conduct—it is only those such as Xu You and Chao Fu who may truly be called "sages."
If one possesses much wisdom but little virtue, they are called a madman; if one possesses much virtue but little wisdom, they are called a fool. Both the mad and the foolish are not sages.

A sage is named for their sagacity and capability, and is also named for their sagacity and goodness. Because they are good, they possess virtue; because they are capable, they possess wisdom. Since they are fully endowed with both wisdom and virtue, they are called a sage (xianren).

The practitioner is likewise: cultivating the wisdom of the four foundations of mindfulness and training in the five concentrations for settling the mind, thereby becoming fully endowed with both concentration and wisdom.
How does counting the breath bring about this full endowment of concentration and wisdom?

To restrain the scattering of discursive thoughts, one proceeds from one to ten, cognizing the breath and its counting; [one realizes] impermanence, arising and ceasing, with every thought-moment never remaining still. Furthermore, if one contemplates impurity, one should feel deep revulsion toward filth and evil;

yet both the observer and the observed are impermanent, subject to arising and ceasing, quickly decaying, empty, and deceptive, deceiving all sentient beings. If, through this contemplation of revulsion, anger arises, one must correspond with the meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*). Seeing others obtain happiness, one likewise knows that this concentration and the characteristics of that happiness are impermanent, subject to arising and ceasing.
When contemplating through causes and conditions, one observes horizontally across the four modes of birth that they are all phenomena produced by causes and conditions;
one observes vertically throughout the three realms that they, too, are phenomena produced by causes and conditions.
Whatever arises from conditions is entirely impermanent and without self.
When various obstacles arise, one must likewise practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
This is called the five cessations (pañca-vyupaśama), which fully cultivate both concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

Because there is concentration, one does not become deranged; because there is wisdom, one does not remain deluded. By relying on this to settle the mind, it serves as the foundation for all practices. It gives rise to the stages of "warmth" (*ūṣmagata*) and "summit" (*mūrdhan*), enters the true illumination of "patience regarding suffering" (*duḥkha-kṣānti*), and becomes a worthy one (*satpuruṣa*) adjacent to the sages. The significance lies precisely here.
This is unlike the non-Buddhists, who do not know how to churn; for them, even the whey is difficult to obtain, let alone the curd or the clarified butter!
Fourth, by universally destroying [deluded] dharmas, one perceives the attainment of the Way; this is the settling of the mind in concentration and wisdom.

If, after the stage of the five objects of stabilization (*pañca-vastu-sthiti-citta*), one cultivates the shared applications of mindfulness (*sādhāraṇa-smṛtyupasthāna*), one universally subdues all phenomena while maintaining [the contemplations of] impurity and so forth; thus both the phenomenal facts (*vastu*) and the principle (*tattva*) are fully accomplished.

If, after the five objects of stabilization, one cultivates the specific applications of mindfulness (*asādhāraṇa-smṛtyupasthāna*) alone, one engages exclusively in contemplation of the principle (*tattvālambana-bhāvanā*), using the wisdom of impermanence to universally subdue all views.
The contemplation for destroying [wrong] views is as elucidated in the final two chapters of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*.

When the Buddha first turned the wheel of Dharma, he did not preach other doctrines, but clarified impermanence alone to universally refute all external paths—whether existence, non-existence, or even neither existence nor non-existence—as well as the self (*ātman*) and the world, permanence and impermanence, and so forth, including the sixty-two views, thereby bringing them to purification.
Now, the Abhidharma masters, having been refuted by others, say:
"Impermanence belongs to the Hīnayāna, while permanence belongs to the Mahāyāna; permanence can refute impermanence, but impermanence cannot refute permanence."
If one were to attain the aforementioned state of mind, this would not be possible;
for prior to attaining the Path, the mind clings to conceptualizations such as permanence, impermanence, both permanence and impermanence, and neither permanence nor impermanence.
When mental objects encounter the mind-faculty, various views arise; these views arise from conditions. That which arises from conditions is entirely impermanent.
How then can non-Buddhists speak of permanence, bliss, self, and purity?
These four inversions are all destroyed by means of impermanence.
Therefore, five hundred bhikṣus said to Dabba:
"By practicing only impermanence, one can attain the Path and can attain the supernormal powers."
"Just as when the group of six bhikṣus teaches the Dharma to others, they speak exclusively of impermanence;
one should know that regardless of whether their insight is deep or shallow, all are undermined by impermanence. This is not like the old physician who used milk medicine exclusively."
Fifth, regarding knowing what is obstructed and what is unobstructed: although the preceding section has universally refuted the faults of various views, their virtues have not yet been seen.
Faults constitute obstruction, while virtues constitute the unobstructed.

If there are the eighty-eight afflictions (*anuśaya*) within the view of existence, up to and including those within the unspeakable view that is neither existence nor non-existence, all of these arise from conditions; they are termed "obstructions," and because they are obstructions, they must be destroyed.

Furthermore, regarding the recognition of that which is penetrating: it refers to the cessation of the middle way through seeing, up to the unutterable cessation of the middle way through neither-existence-nor-non-existence. Such a cessation of the path arises from causes and conditions; this is called "penetration. Why, then, must penetration be refuted?

If one does not recognize these various views, but instead claims that this alone is reality while all else is false speech, then by clinging to such views one creates karma; when moistened by craving, this leads to the ripening of karmic fruits—is this not indeed a state of obstruction?
One is able to recognize that each and every view is impermanent and inverted; by not giving rise to attachment and not clinging, there is no karma; and where there is no karma, there is no fruit.
One who attains such realization has realized the cessation of the path; how could this not be called penetration?
This is unlike the non-Buddhists, who are like insects boring through wood; these insects do not know whether what they have gnawed is a character or not.
Sixth, regarding those who skillfully cultivate the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*): how could they merely recognize these points of penetration and obstruction?
They must cultivate the factors of enlightenment and advance through the various gateways of the Dharma.

That is to say, observing that this "view of existence," up to and including the "inexpressible view," all depend upon form (*rūpa*) and are defiled and impure—this is the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).

Whether one experiences feeling, up to and including experiencing inexpressible feeling, all are based on the three types of feeling; since feeling itself is suffering, this is called the foundation of mindfulness of feeling (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*).
To contemplate that the perceptions and mental formations arising from various views are entirely without self is called the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*).
To contemplate the mind of various views as being impermanent from moment to moment is called the application of mindfulness to the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*).

To contemplate these four contemplations is called attaining right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*) within conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*); because one attains this mindfulness, the four inversions (*viparyāsa*) are subdued, and this is termed the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Diligently cultivating the four contemplations is called the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).
Cultivating them within a concentrated mind is called the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*).
Because the five wholesome roots arise, they are called the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).
The five faculties increase and obstruct all unwholesome dharmas; therefore, they are called the five powers (*pañcabala*).
The harmonious balancing of concentration and wisdom is called the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).
Proceeding upon the path of peace and security is called the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).
This is not a discussion of the factors of enlightenment according to their specific stages; rather, it concerns the thirty-seven factors as they are cultivated in common.
If one application of the mind constitutes the thirty-seven factors, the same applies to all other applications of the mind.
In the *Abhidharma*, within the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*), this should be analyzed in detail, and so forth.

These thirty-seven factors are the dharmas for practicing the path; they lead one toward the city of Nirvāṇa, which has three gates. Specifically, the two modes of practice belonging to the category of suffering constitute the gate of liberation through emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*).
The four aspects of each of the [three] truths regarding the path constitute the gate of wishlessness (*apranihita-vimokṣamukha*). Below the truth of suffering there are two;
this is the gate of wishlessness. Below the truth of cessation there are four; this is the gate of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*).
When the gate of nirvana opens, one immediately enters it.

Therefore, in the *Subhadra-sūtra*, the Buddha made this definitive lion’s roar: "Only within my Dharma is there the Eightfold Noble Path; even a single path does not exist within the teachings of the outsiders, let alone the Eightfold Path."

Seventh, regarding the skillful cultivation of remedies: if a person of sharp faculties enters [the path] immediately, but if they do not enter, they should cultivate the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
Thus, the Treatise says:
"The twelve dhyānas and so forth are all methods for opening the gate; since right wisdom is weak, hindrances arise, and one cultivates the factors conducive to enlightenment as an aid."
The Treatise says:
"When greed arises, one teaches the cultivation of the contemplation of impurity, the stages of liberation, and so forth;
when there is no mastery over objects, one should teach the spheres of mastery."
If one's conditions are not extensive and universal, one should teach [the practice] for all places.
If one has little merit, one should teach the immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa-citta*).
If one wishes to transcend the form realm, one should teach the four formless attainments (*catasra ārūpyasamāpattayaḥ*).
All such things as these are aids to the Path and methods for opening the gate; they are not like the outsiders who, regarding fundamental dhyāna, give rise to craving, views, and pride.

Eighth, regarding being well-versed in the stages and positions: although one may practice such dharmas as the primary and auxiliary methods, one must not immediately claim, "I am a sage. To do so would be to arrogantly overstep the distinction between the true and the semblance, failing to recognize the difference between the worthy and the holy.
Now, by clearly discerning the distinction between the true and the semblance, and knowing for oneself that one is not a sage, the pride of superiority cannot arise.
This is unlike the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), who, through the grasping at precepts and views, reckon the phenomena of birth and death to be *nirvāṇa*.
9. Skillfully Cultivating Patience.
When the power of the specific-characteristic foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) is weak, they have not yet become thoroughly pervasive and relaxed.

One should then cultivate the general-characteristic foundations of mindfulness—whether by combining one, two, or even all four. At this time, one must exercise patience so that the contemplation may reach fulfillment and progress into the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), where a semblance of the path arises like smoke.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"Although 'Heat' (*uṣmagata*) is itself outflowing (*sāsrava*) and conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is nevertheless able to destroy that which is outflowing and conditioned.
"My disciples possess this; the non-Buddhists do not."

Furthermore, if patience (*kṣānti*) is perfected, it becomes the stage of the Summits (*mūrdhan*); when the Summits are perfected, they become patience. Upon reaching the edge, if one is not patient, one retreats back to this side.
Therefore it is said:
"Falling back from the stage of the Summits constitutes the five heinous crimes; falling back from the stage of Heat constitutes an icchantika.
For this reason, one must here properly cultivate patience regarding all internal and external obstacles, unlike the non-Buddhists who are unable to endure even subtle hindrances.

10. Regarding the non-arising of craving for dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*): since one has already attained the arising of the four roots of goodness (*catvāri kuśalamūlāni*) as described above, if one were to give rise to craving for dharmas, although one would not fall back into the state of the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) or the icchantika, one would still be unable to enter the realization of the truths (*satyadarśana*).

This constitutes the three stages of the contemplation of contraction (*saṃkṣepa-vipaśyanā*), which advances to the stage of "superior patience" (*adhimātra-kṣānti*). From the "highest worldly dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*), the true illumination of the "patience regarding suffering" (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) arises; within sixteen moments, one attains the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), or perhaps attains a "leap-over fruit" (*vyutkrāntaka-phala*);
or, by employing the contemplation repeatedly, one cuts off the five lower and five upper fetters, thereby attaining the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
If those of sharp faculties employ contemplation, they attain entry stage by stage;
if those of dull faculties employ contemplation, it must proceed through all stages up to the tenth.
Although the Abhidharma provides extensive explanations, they do not go beyond these ten points.

The five hundred Arhats composed the *Vibhāṣā*, wherein they correctly expounded that one attains the Way through the gate of existence (*astivāda*). How can it be said that this is merely a skillful means for disciplining the mind?
Through the harmonious application of all four gates, one is equally able to attain the Way.
If one gives rise to attachment, in either case one will not attain the Way.
If you claim that seeing existence leads to the attainment of the Way while seeing emptiness does not, how does this differ from the non-Buddhists?
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"If one does not obtain the skillful means (*upāya*) of Prajñā, one falls into the extremes of existence and non-existence.
Now, by taking these ten dharmas as skillful means, one enters directly through the gate of Truth, forever distinguishing oneself from the heterodox paths.
This is the contemplation for entering reality by way of the gate of existence.

As for the other gates—the gate of emptiness, the gate of both emptiness and existence, and the gate of neither emptiness nor existence—they are all skillful means from beginning to end for entering reality; yet, compared to the gate of existence, each is distinct.
Nevertheless, they all converge upon the partial truth (pratisaṃvid-satya) and sever the delusions of the three realms; there is no difference between them.

These three gates correspond to the [standard] sequence and should follow the pattern of the Ten Contemplations; they are largely the same with minor differences that can be understood through one's own reflection. I shall not trouble myself here to record them in detail.
Next, to clarify the contemplation of the "Gate of Existence" (yu-men) within the Shared Teaching (tongjiao), there are ten points, the titles of which are listed as follows.
One realizes that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations.
"Although the three types of persons are alike in their initial resolve, there are also slight differences between them," and so forth.
